strategies.summary: In inference (eval) mode, BatchNorm is a pure per-channel affine: fold bn_weight, bn_bias, running_mean, running_var, eps, divide_value, and extra_bias into two precomputed vectorsâeffective_scale[c] and effective_bias[c]âcached on first call. Then the entire post-GEMM computation collapses to one vectorized kernel: out[i,c] = swish(x[i,c] * eff_scale[c] + eff_bias[c]), using float4 loads/stores on the [N,C] tensor with C innermost. This eliminates the two-pass BN stats kernel entirely in eval mode and reduces post-GEMM memory traffic to a single round-trip.
implementation_hints: Cache the precomputed (effective_scale, effective_bias) tensors on the module; invalidate when bn.running_mean or bn.running_var is updated (track a version counter or recompute at each eval forward cheaply).

effective_scale[c] = bn_weight[c] / sqrt(running_var[c] + eps) / divide_value; effective_bias[c] = (bn_bias[c] - running_mean[c] * effective_scale[c]) / divide_value + extra_bias_broadcast[c] / divide_valueâhandle numel==1 broadcast for extra_bias.

In the CUDA kernel use a float4 load on x (assert C % 4 == 0 or handle tail), loadeff_scale[c:c+4] and eff_bias[c:c+4] from __ldg, apply per-lane affine, compute swish = v * (1.f / (1.f + __expf(-v))), store float4.
Launch with1D grid: blocks = (N*C/4+ THREADS - 1) / THREADS, threads = 256. Each thread processes 4 consecutive elements in the C dimension.
Keep training-mode fallback using the existing two-pass kernel or torch.nn.functional.batch_norm to preserve correctness.
Guard the fast path: bn.training == False, x.is_contiguous(), x.dtype == float32, C % 4 == 0.
strategies.expected_gain: Eliminates the two-pass BN stats kernel in eval mode; post-GEMM kernel becomes a single bandwidth-limited pass at ~2x fewer memory transactions via float4. NCU L2 throughput at 64.32% suggests the post-BN kernel is near cache-bandwidth ceiling; vectorization and parameter folding reduce transaction count by ~5x (no separate mean/var/weight/bias loads per-element). Projected5â12% total speedup on top of current 1.033x, depending on how much post-BN time remains.
risk_notes: Only valid when bn.training == False; must detect mode switch and recompute precomputed vectors.
extra_bias with numel==1 vs numel==C must both be handled before precomputation.
C % 4 alignment must be verified at runtime; use scalar fallback for misaligned tail.
Do not change running_mean/running_var update semantics in training mode.
forbidden_patterns: recomputing running stats in eval mode
separate bias+divide+swish kernel launches
scalar element-wise loads in the apply kernel

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very useful for eval workloads. Folding running-stat BN plus divide/bias into cached per-channel affine vectors is mathematically sound in eval mode and yields a simple single-pass epilogue. Requires careful cache invalidation and guards, but risk is well contained.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Highest risk-adjusted value in the portfolio. Parameter folding in eval mode eliminates the two-pass BN kernel entirely and float4 vectorization directly addresses the 64.32% L2 throughput observation. Implementation is well-scoped: precompute two vectors, one vectorized kernel, guard on bn.training and C%4. Mode detection and broadcast handling for extra_bias (numel==1 vs numel==C) are the only real risks and both are explicitly called out with mitigations.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Precomputing the effective scale and bias for eval mode and utilizing float4 vectorization will maximize memory bandwidth utilization, which is critical for elementwise epilogues.

implementation_hints: Keep `forward_stmt_1` on the vendor GEMM; only change the guarded fused call site and CUDA entrypoints.
Add an eval-specialized kernel that reads `running_mean`/`running_var` directly and skips temporary `mean_t`/`var_t` allocation and batch-stat reduction.
Retain a training-specialized path that computes batch mean/variance over the exact N axis for each channel and then applies affine, extra bias, divide, and Swish.
Use separate exported entrypoints or an internal dispatch to avoid runtime branching inside the hot kernel.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Strong risk-adjusted choice. Cleanly separates eval and training semantics, preserves exact BatchNorm axes/behavior, and removes unnecessary stats work in eval without touching the GEMM. Good upside with manageable implementation complexity.

Low implementation risk since it avoids the more complex weight-folding or cublasLt paths. Solid foundational improvement that complements strategies 02 and 05.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Excellent approach to separate eval and training paths. In eval mode, BatchNorm is purely an elementwise affine transform, so a single-pass fused epilogue is highly optimal.

strategies.summary: Fix the critical serial bottleneck in the current bn_stats_kernel: it assigns one channel per thread and loops over N=1024 rowsâall serial within a thread. Replace it with one CUDA block per channel (8192 blocks), each doing a parallel reduction over N=1024 elements using warp shuffles(__shfl_down_sync), eliminating the serial loop. Pair this with a float4-vectorized bn_apply_kernel to reduce L2 memory transaction count by 4x. This directly addresses the 64.32% L2 throughput and low occupancy (32.49%) seen in the NCU profile.
implementation_hints: bn_stats_kernel: launch grid of (C, 1) blocks, each with 256 threads. Each thread accumulates elements x[t::256, c] for t in 0..255, then performs a two-level warp+block reduction using __shfl_down_sync and shared memory. Store mean and var per channel.

Use Welford's online algorithm within each thread to avoid catastrophic cancellation on large N: maintain (count, mean_acc, M2) per thread, then combine partial Welford accumulators during the warp reduction phase.

bn_apply_kernel: require C % 4 == 0 and cast x, out pointers to float4. Each thread handles4 consecutive C-dimension elements: load float4 x_vec, load float4 scale_vec/bias_vec via __ldg, apply swish, store float4.
Launch bn_apply with grid = (N * C / 4 + 255) / 256 blocks of 256 threads.

For the combined scale/bias load in the apply kernel, precompute inv_std = rsqrt(var + eps) and store weight*inv_std and (bn_bias - mean*weight*inv_std + extra_bias) / divide_value as packed float4 arrays before launching the apply kernel.
strategies.expected_gain: The parallel block reduction replaces 1024 serial iterations per thread with a log2(1024)=10-step reduction; expected 10â50x speedup on the stats kernel alone. Float4 vectorization reduces memory transactions 4x for the apply kernel. Combined, this should reduce post-GEMM kernel time significantly. Since the GEMM dominates total time, overall projected gain is 3â8% on top of current 1.033x.
risk_notes: Welford accumulator combination across warps requires careful shared memory layout to avoid bank conflicts.
C % 4 == 0 must be verified; for C=8192 (current) this holds, but add a runtime guard.
Block reduction requires __syncthreads between warp-level and block-level reduction stages.
Training mode Bessel correction (N/(N-1)) must still be applied when updating running_var.
forbidden_patterns: one_channel_per_thread_serial_loop_over_N
scalar_element_wise_loads_in_apply
separate_kernel_for_inv_std_computation

review_notes.openai-compatible: Practical and targeted. Parallel Welford reduction for per-channel stats directly fixes the obvious serial bottleneck, and float4 apply vectorization is a reasonable complement. Main risks are reduction correctness and engineering detail, but overall value is good.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Well-specified and directly targets the identified serial bottleneck: one-channel-per-thread looping over N=1024 rows. The parallel block reduction with Welford accumulators and float4 apply is a principled fix. Welford combiner across warps requires careful shared memory layout but the implementation hints are concrete enough to execute correctly. Gain is real for training mode though GEMM still dominates total wall time.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Provides a concrete and highly effective plan for parallel block reduction and vectorized apply, directly addressing potential bottlenecks in the stats computation.

strategies.summary: Replace torch.nn.Linear's internal cuBLAS sgemm call with an explicit cublasLtMatmul that carries a fused BIAS epilogue, and pre-fold the eval-mode BN affine transform into the Linear weight matrix and bias vector before the matmul. The net result is the GEMM writes affine-normalized values directly, and a single lightweight Swish kernel (or cuBLASLt's epilogue path) finishes the computation. This targets the dominant ampere_sgemm_128x128_tn kernel by reducing the total number of kernel launches and avoiding a full re-read of the [1024,8192] output.
implementation_hints: In eval mode, precompute a scaled weight matrix: W_eff = diag(eff_scale) @ self.matmul.weight, and a scalar bias b_eff = eff_scale * matmul.bias +eff_bias (per-channel). Store these as buffers updated on eval() calls.
Call cublasLtMatmul with CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BIAS to add b_eff in the epilogue, then run a minimal Swish kernel on the output. This cuts post-GEMM kernel launches to 1.
Alternatively, if cublasLt epilogue support for custom activations is unavailable, use the scaled-weight path with a single vectorized Swish kernel (float4) as a follow-on.
Use AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES to stay fp32-only for the cuBLAS path.
Provide a clean fallback: if precomputed buffers are stale (training mode or parameter update), fall back to the existing fused BN path from n4.
Register scaled weight/bias as non-leaf buffers (register_buffer) to avoid gradient computation.
strategies.expected_gain: Eliminates the separate post-GEMM BN normalization kernel entirely in eval mode. The GEMM is already72.5% SM throughput; by fusing the affine into the weight matrix, the only overhead after the GEMM is a single Swish kernel (~0.5% of compute). Expected 8â15% total speedup in eval mode from removing2 kernel launches and 2 full tensor reads.
risk_notes: Weight folding is only valid in eval mode; must re-derive when switching to training.
cublasLtMatmul requires careful workspace sizing and handle initializationâuse a singleton handle.
Row vs column major layout conventions must match the TN layout used by ampere_sgemm_128x128_tn.
Bessel correction and running_var updates in training mode must still use the unfused BN path.
forbidden_patterns: modifying model weight parameters in-place during forward
calling self.bn() after weight folding without resetting
using cuBLAS workspace larger than L2 cache size

review_notes.openai-compatible: Potentially high payoff, but materially higher integration risk. Replacing the existing Linear path with explicit cublasLt and folded weights adds layout, buffer-staleness, and maintenance hazards. Good idea for a dedicated inference path, but weaker risk-adjusted value than simpler eval epilogues.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Highest theoretical ceiling (fusing affine into GEMM weight matrix eliminates the BN kernel entirely) but also highest implementation risk. cublasLtMatmul requires careful handle lifecycle, workspace sizing, and TN layout matching. Weight matrix rescaling must be invalidated correctly on mode switches and parameter updates. The correctness surface is large enough that a misimplementation could silently produce wrong results. Recommend only after strategies 01 and 02 are validated.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Folding the BN affine parameters into the GEMM weights is mathematically optimal for eval mode and eliminates the BN read entirely. Managing the precomputed weights adds slight complexity but offers great speedup.

strategies.summary: The NCU profile shows launch__occupancy_limit_registers: 2, meaning118 registers/thread in the ampere_sgemm kernel limits occupancy to only 2 warps/SM (32.49% active warps). While the GEMM itself is a vendor kernel and cannot be modified, the custom post-GEMM kernels should be tuned to maximize their own occupancy to overlap with any concurrent execution. Use __launch_bounds__(256, 4) on the bn_apply_kernel to force the compiler to target 4 warps/SM, reducing register spills. Additionally, split the combined affine+swish computation across two warps using warp specialization if register count remains high, and use __maxrregcount compile flag to cap custom kernel register usage at 64.
implementation_hints: Annotate bn_apply_kernel with __launch_bounds__(256, 4) to hint the compiler to keep registers below 32per thread for4-warp occupancy target.
Add --maxrregcount=64 to extra_cuda_cflags in load_inline to globally cap register use of custom kernels.
In bn_stats_kernel, use __launch_bounds__(256, 8) since the stats kernel has simpler arithmetic and can afford higher occupancy targets.
Profile the apply kernel independently: if arithmetic intensity is low (as expected for affine+swish), higher occupancy from fewer registers will improve memory latency hiding.

Consider splitting the swish computation: one warp writes the affine result, another reads and applies sigmoidâthis is only worthwhile if register pressure is the confirmed bottleneck in the custom kernel, not the GEMM.
Add --generate-line-info to cuda_cflags during development to confirm register allocation via nvcc --ptxas-options=-v.
strategies.expected_gain: The GEMM kernel's low occupancy (32.49%) is fixed by cuBLAS and cannot be changed, but ensuring custom kernels run at higher occupancy improves their memory latency tolerance. The smsp__warp_issue_stalled_not_selected ratio of 0.35 indicates substantial issue slot waste which correlates with low warp count. Projected 2â5% gain on the custom kernel portion; marginal total speedup but important as a correctness-preserving foundation for other strategies.
risk_notes: __launch_bounds__ can cause register spilling to local memory if the constraint is too tight, which is worse than moderate register usageâprofile with nvcc --ptxas-options=-v to confirm no spilling.
--maxrregcount affects all kernels in the translation unit; if bn_stats uses complex reductions, capping too low causes spills.
Do not apply these flags to the GEMM path; they only affect custom CUDA sources in cuda_cu.
This is a secondary optimization; prefer strategies1 or 2 first as they have higher ceiling gains.
forbidden_patterns: applying maxrregcount to vendor GEMM paths
launch_bounds tighter than kernel arithmetic allows without profiling
warp specialization without profiling confirming register is the bottleneck

review_notes.openai-compatible: High tuning risk for modest expected value. Forcing register limits and launch bounds can easily backfire via spills, and the cited occupancy issue mostly concerns vendor GEMM that cannot be changed here. Better as a follow-up profiling exercise than a primary strategy.
review_notes.claude-compatible: __launch_bounds__ and --maxrregcount are important hygiene for ensuring custom kernels do not waste SM resources, but the GEMM occupancy limit (32.49%) is fixed by cuBLAS and cannot be influenced by these flags. Risk of register spilling if constraints are set too aggressively without profiling nvcc --ptxas-options=-v first. Best used as a compile-time guard alongside strategies 02 or 05, not as a standalone improvement.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Register tuning via launch bounds is a low-level micro-optimization with potential risks (e.g., register spilling) and limited upside compared to algorithmic changes.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l2_p97_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():

phase2_n1.performance_hypothesis: The current bottleneck inside the custom fused path is the training-mode stats pass, where each thread serially scans all `N=1024` rows for one channel. A CTA-per-channel Welford reduction plus a float4 apply fastpath will materially reduce custom-kernel time without altering the working Python/C++ dispatch structure.

Replace the CUDA source so it retains the current training/general fused implementation, but adds an eval-specialized path: (1) add a kernel that computes `out[idx] = swish(x[idx] * eff_scale[c] + eff_bias[c])` where `c = idx % C`; vectorize with `float4` when `C % 4 == 0`, with a scalar fallback for tails or unsupported alignment; (2) in the new exported eval wrapper, allocate contiguous `eff_scale` and `eff_bias` tensors of length `C`, compute `inv_std = rsqrt(running_var + eps)`, then compute `eff_scale = weight * inv_std / divide_value` and `eff_bias = (bias - running_mean * weight * inv_std + extra_bias_broadcast) / divide_value`; handle `extra_bias.numel()==1` by filling with the scalar, and `numel()==C` by channel-wise use; (3) launch only the eval apply kernel and return `out`; (4) keep the existing training/general wrapper and kernels available for `bn.training == True`, without changing training semantics or normalized axes.

Replace the guarded fused-call block so it first checks the existing CUDA/float32/contiguous/2D/bias-shape conditions, then dispatches to `_stark_get_extension().matmul_batchnorm_biasadd_divide_swish_eval(...)` when `not self.bn.training`, otherwise dispatches to the existing `_stark_get_extension().matmul_batchnorm_biasadd_divide_swish(...)`; keep `fused_done = True` only on successful extension calls, and keep the current exact-PyTorch fallback `x = self.bn(x)` on any exception or unsupported case.

Replace the CUDA helper region by preserving the current training-capable fused implementation, then add a separate eval kernel path: (1) add a kernel that computes `out = swish(x * eff_scale + eff_bias)` over contiguous `[N,C]` data using a float4 fastpath when `C % 4 == 0` and pointers are 16-byte aligned, with scalar fallback otherwise; (2) in the new exported eval wrapper, validate CUDA/float32/2D/contiguous inputs and `extra_bias.numel() in {1, C}`, compute per-channel `eff_scale = weight / sqrt(running_var + eps) / divide_value` and `eff_bias = bias - running_mean * weight / sqrt(running_var + eps)`, then fold `extra_bias` and final divide so the kernel only reads `x`, `eff_scale`, and `eff_bias`; handle both scalar and channel-wise `extra_bias` correctly; (3) keep the existing training wrapper behavior unchanged for `training == true`.

Replace the guarded fused-call block so that after `x = self.matmul(x)`, it first checks the existing CUDA/float32/2D/contiguous/bias-shape guards; if valid and `self.bn.training` is `False`, call `_stark_get_extension().matmul_batchnorm_biasadd_divide_swish_eval(x, self.bn.running_mean, self.bn.running_var, self.bn.weight, self.bn.bias, self.bias.reshape(-1) if self.bias.numel() > 1 else self.bias.view(1), self.bn.eps, float(self.divide_value))` and set `fused_done = True`; otherwise, in training mode call the existing `_stark_get_extension().matmul_batchnorm_biasadd_divide_swish(...)`; on exception, fall back to `x = self.bn(x)` and leave `fused_done = False`.
